assessment.name: Year 10 Autumn Science Assessment (Physics part)
assessment.sections: Thursday 3 December, period 2. Section A: 45 multiple choice questions online across biology, chemistry and physics. Section B: written answers.
assessment.weighting: 60% this term's unit P4.1 Matter. 40% Year 9 units: energy and electricity, thermal physics, forces and motion, waves.
assessment.equipment: Chromebook, black pen, pencil, ruler, calculator

mock.note: 15 physics questions weighted 60/40. Do the biology and chemistry mocks too for the full 45.

leitner_plan.new: P4.1 fluids and atmosphere, energy and electricity (7)
Homework booklet topics: energy, heating, EM waves (6)

cards.title: Density
cards.question: What is density, and how does the particle model explain why solids are usually denser than gases?
points: density (kg/m³) = mass (kg) ÷ volume (m³), ρ = m ÷ V
Solids and liquids have particles close together, so they are much denser than gases.
1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
Changes of state conserve mass. The volume changes, so the density changes.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A 2.7 kg block has a volume of 0.001 m³

cards.watch_out: Convert cm³ to m³ by dividing by 1 000 000, not 1000.
cards.hook: Density triangle: M on top, D and V underneath (Mr Dave).
cards.grade9: Rearrange confidently, V = m ÷ ρ, and give answers in standard form when needed.

cards.title: Density required practical
cards.question: How do you measure the density of a regular solid, an irregular solid and a liquid?
points: Regular solid: measure length, width and height with a ruler, volume = l × w × h, mass on a balance.
Irregular solid: lower it into a full eureka (displacement) can and measure the overflow in a measuring cylinder.
Liquid: measure the mass of an empty cylinder, add a known volume, measure again; subtract.
Repeat and calculate a mean to reduce the effect of random errors.
cards.watch_out: Read the measuring cylinder at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus.
cards.grade9: Name a source of error (water stuck to the object, a gap in the eureka can spout) and how to reduce it.

cards.title: Particle motion in gases
cards.question: How does the particle model explain gas temperature and pressure?
points: Gas particles move randomly at high speed and collide with each other and the container walls.
The temperature of a gas is related to the average kinetic energy of its particles.
Collisions with the walls exert a force, causing pressure.
At constant volume, heating a gas makes particles move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often; pressure rises.
cards.watch_out: Pressure rises because of more frequent and harder collisions, both points.
cards.grade9: Link each step, temperature up, kinetic energy up, speed up, more frequent and more forceful collisions, pressure up.

cards.title: Pressure and volume of a gas (separate)
cards.question: How does the pressure of a fixed mass of gas change with volume at constant temperature?
points: The force from gas pressure acts at right angles (normal) to the container walls.
At constant temperature, increasing the volume means particles hit the walls less often, so pressure falls.
pV = constant (pressure × volume stays the same), for a fixed mass at constant temperature.
cards.watch_out: pV = constant only works if temperature does not change.
cards.hook: Squeeze it smaller, push it harder: p up, V down.
cards.grade9: Use p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ and keep the same pressure units on both sides.

cards.title: Doing work on a gas (higher, separate)
cards.question: Why does pumping up a bike tyre make the pump warm?
points: Work is done on a gas when it is compressed.
This transfers energy to the gas, increasing its internal energy.
The particles move faster, so the temperature of the gas rises.
cards.watch_out: The temperature rise is from work done, not from friction alone.
cards.grade9: Use the chain, work done, energy transferred, internal energy up, average kinetic energy up, temperature up.

cards.title: Pressure in a fluid
cards.question: How do you calculate pressure in a fluid, and why does it increase with depth?
points: pressure (Pa) = force normal to a surface (N) ÷ area (m²), p = F ÷ A
Fluids (liquids and gases) exert pressure in all directions, at right angles to any surface.
Pressure due to a column of liquid: p = h × ρ × g (height × density × gravitational field strength).
Pressure increases with depth because there is more liquid above pushing down. Denser liquids give more pressure.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: 10 m of water, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg

cards.watch_out: 1 Pa = 1 N/m². Make sure area is in m².
cards.grade9: Explain upthrust from the pressure difference between the top and bottom of an object.

cards.title: Upthrust and floating (separate)
cards.question: What causes upthrust, and why do some objects float?
points: A submerged object has greater pressure on its bottom surface than its top, because the bottom is deeper.
This gives a resultant upward force called upthrust.
Upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.
An object floats when its weight equals the upthrust. Objects less dense than the fluid float; denser objects sink.
cards.watch_out: Upthrust depends on the volume submerged, not the object's own density.
cards.grade9: Explain why a steel ship floats, its shape displaces a large volume of water, so upthrust can equal its weight.

cards.title: Atmospheric pressure (separate)
cards.question: What causes atmospheric pressure, and why does it decrease with height?
points: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air round the Earth that gets less dense with height.
Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure.
With increasing height there is less air above, so fewer molecules and a lower weight of air, giving lower pressure.
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 100 000 Pa (100 kPa).
cards.watch_out: Atmospheric pressure acts in all directions, not just downwards.
cards.grade9: Use two reasons for the decrease, less air above and lower density of air.

cards.title: National and global energy resources
cards.question: What are the main energy resources, and how do renewable and non-renewable sources compare?
points: Non-renewable: coal, oil, gas, nuclear. Reliable but will run out; fossil fuels release CO₂.
Renewable: wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, waves, geothermal, biofuel. Will not run out but some are unreliable (weather dependent).
Transport mainly uses oil-based fuels. Heating uses gas and electricity.
The UK is increasing renewables, but this costs money and some people object to how they look or where they are sited.
cards.watch_out: Nuclear is non-renewable and does not release CO₂ when running.
cards.grade9: Evaluate using reliability, cost, environmental impact and how quickly supply can be increased.

cards.title: AC, DC and mains electricity
cards.question: What is the difference between alternating and direct current, and what do the wires in a plug do?
points: Direct potential difference (cells, batteries) gives current in one direction only.
Mains electricity in the UK is alternating current, 230 V at 50 Hz.
Live wire (brown): carries 230 V. Neutral (blue): completes the circuit, about 0 V. Earth (green and yellow): safety, carries current only if there is a fault.
Touching a live wire is dangerous even when a switch is off, because your body is at 0 V and current flows through you.
cards.watch_out: The earth wire stops the case becoming live; the fuse then melts.
cards.hook: BRown = BRight live, BLue = BeLow (neutral), green-yellow = ground (earth).
cards.grade9: Explain danger through potential difference between the live wire and you.

cards.title: Power and energy transfer
cards.question: How do you calculate power and energy transferred in a circuit?
points: P = E ÷ t (power in W, energy in J, time in s)
P = I × V and P = I² × R
E = Q × V (energy = charge × potential difference) and E = P × t
Appliances transfer energy from the mains, for example to the kinetic store of a motor or the thermal store of a kettle.
cards.watch_out: Time must be in seconds. Convert minutes by multiplying by 60.
cards.grade9: Pick the right power equation by looking at which two quantities you are given.

cards.title: The National Grid
cards.question: How does the National Grid use transformers to transfer energy efficiently?
points: The National Grid is a system of cables and transformers linking power stations to consumers.
Step-up transformers increase the pd to very high values for transmission. This lowers the current.
A lower current means less energy lost as heat in the cables (P = I²R), so it is more efficient.
Step-down transformers reduce the pd to a safe 230 V for homes.
cards.watch_out: High voltage, low current. Losses depend on current squared.
cards.grade9: Use P = I²R to explain why halving the current quarters the power loss.

cards.title: Changes of state and internal energy
cards.question: What is internal energy, and what happens to it during a change of state?
points: Internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles in a system.
Heating increases internal energy, either raising the temperature or changing the state.
Changes of state are physical changes and are reversible. Mass is conserved.
During a change of state the temperature stays the same; energy breaks bonds between particles (potential energy).
cards.watch_out: Temperature is linked only to kinetic energy, not total internal energy.
cards.grade9: Explain the flat part of a heating curve, energy goes into potential energy, not kinetic energy.

cards.title: Specific heat capacity
cards.question: What is specific heat capacity, and how do you use ΔE = m c Δθ?
points: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.
ΔE (J) = m (kg) × c (J/kg °C) × Δθ (°C)
Water has a high specific heat capacity, about 4200 J/kg °C.
Required practical: heat a block with a heater, measure energy with a joulemeter (or P × t) and the temperature rise; insulate the block.
cards.watch_out: Δθ is the change in temperature, not the final temperature.
cards.hook: mcat: ΔE = m c Δθ (m-c-theta sounds like 'emcat').
cards.grade9: Explain why the measured c is often too high, energy lost to the surroundings.

cards.title: Specific latent heat
cards.question: What is specific latent heat, and how do you calculate the energy to melt or boil a substance?
points: Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance with no change in temperature.
E (J) = m (kg) × L (J/kg)
Fusion: solid ↔ liquid. Vaporisation: liquid ↔ gas.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Melt 0.5 kg of ice, L = 334 000 J/kg

cards.watch_out: Use L only for the flat parts of a heating graph; use mcΔθ for the sloping parts.
cards.grade9: In multi-step questions, add the energy for each stage of the heating curve.

cards.title: Scalars, vectors and forces
cards.question: What is the difference between scalar and vector quantities, and between contact and non-contact forces?
points: Scalars have size (magnitude) only. Vectors have magnitude and direction. Vectors are drawn as arrows.
Scalars: distance, speed, mass, time, energy. Vectors: displacement, velocity, force, acceleration, momentum.
Contact forces: friction, air resistance, tension, normal contact force. Non-contact: gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic.
cards.watch_out: Weight is a force (vector). Mass is a scalar.
cards.hook: Vectors have a Very clear direction.
cards.grade9: Classify pairs correctly in one line, for example speed is the scalar, velocity the vector.

cards.title: Gravity and weight
cards.question: How do you calculate weight, and what is the centre of mass?
points: W = m × g (weight in N, mass in kg, g in N/kg). On Earth g = 9.8 N/kg.
Weight is the force due to gravity and acts at the object's centre of mass.
Weight is measured with a calibrated spring balance (newtonmeter).
Weight is directly proportional to mass.
cards.watch_out: Use g = 9.8 N/kg unless the question gives 10.
cards.grade9: Write W ∝ m and say what proportional means with an example.

cards.title: Resultant forces and free body diagrams
cards.question: How do you find the resultant force, and what does a free body diagram show?
points: The resultant force is the single force with the same effect as all the forces acting together.
Forces in the same direction add; in opposite directions subtract.
A free body diagram shows all forces on an object as labelled arrows from its centre.
Balanced forces give a resultant of zero.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Thrust 500 N forwards, drag 350 N backwards

cards.watch_out: Always give the direction of a resultant force.
cards.grade9: For forces at angles (higher), use a scale drawing to find the resultant.

cards.title: Distance, displacement, speed and velocity
cards.question: What is the difference between distance and displacement, and between speed and velocity?
points: Distance is how far something moves (scalar). Displacement is distance in a stated direction (vector).
speed = distance ÷ time, s = v × t
Velocity is speed in a given direction. An object moving in a circle at constant speed has a changing velocity.
Typical speeds: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s, sound in air 330 m/s.
cards.watch_out: Going round a full lap gives a displacement of zero.
cards.grade9: Use typical speeds to estimate answers and check if a calculated value is sensible.

cards.title: Distance-time graphs
cards.question: How do you find speed from a distance-time graph, including when it curves?
points: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed.
A straight line means constant speed. A flat line means stationary.
A curve means changing speed. Find the speed at an instant by drawing a tangent and finding its gradient (higher).
cards.watch_out: Use a large triangle when finding a gradient to reduce reading errors.
cards.grade9: Show the tangent and the triangle on the graph; the drawing earns marks.

cards.title: Acceleration
cards.question: How do you calculate acceleration, and what do velocity-time graphs show?
points: a = Δv ÷ t (acceleration in m/s², change in velocity in m/s, time in s)
v² − u² = 2 a s (final velocity, initial velocity, acceleration, distance)
The gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration. The area under it is distance travelled.
Objects falling freely near the Earth accelerate at about 9.8 m/s².

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Car goes from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4 s

cards.watch_out: Deceleration gives a negative acceleration.
cards.hook: VTGA: on a Velocity-Time graph, Gradient = Acceleration, Area = distance.
cards.grade9: Use v² − u² = 2as when time is not given. Rearrange before substituting.

cards.title: Newton's first and third laws
cards.question: What do Newton's first and third laws state?
points: First law: if the resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays still and a moving object keeps the same velocity.
A resultant force changes speed or direction (or both).
Inertia is the tendency of objects to keep their state of motion.
Third law: when two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other, of the same type.
cards.watch_out: Third law pairs act on different objects, so they never cancel out.
cards.grade9: Do not confuse a third law pair with balanced forces on one object, for example weight and normal force on a book are not a pair.

cards.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
cards.question: What is the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves?
points: Waves transfer energy, not matter.
Transverse: oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, for example ripples on water and all electromagnetic waves.
Longitudinal: oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer, with compressions and rarefactions, for example sound.
cards.watch_out: In a ripple the water moves up and down; it is the wave that moves forward.
cards.hook: Longitudinal = along. Transverse = across (like a T).
cards.grade9: Give evidence that the medium does not travel, such as a cork bobbing in place.

cards.title: Properties of waves
cards.question: What are amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, and how do you calculate wave speed?
points: Amplitude: maximum displacement from rest. Wavelength: distance from one point to the same point on the next wave.
Frequency: waves passing a point each second, in hertz (Hz). Period T = 1 ÷ f.
wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m), v = f λ
Measure the speed of sound with two microphones or by timing an echo; ripples with a ripple tank and strobe.
cards.watch_out: Convert kHz to Hz (× 1000) and cm to m (÷ 100).
cards.grade9: Explain how to make measurements more accurate, such as timing many waves and dividing.

cards.title: Physics equations to recall
cards.question: Can you write each equation and its units from memory?
points: ρ = m ÷ V; p = F ÷ A; W = m g
P = E ÷ t; P = I V; P = I² R; E = Q V
s = v t; a = Δv ÷ t; v = f λ
Given on the sheet: ΔE = m c Δθ; E = m L; v² − u² = 2 a s; p = h ρ g
cards.watch_out: Learn which are given on the equation sheet and which you must recall.
cards.grade9: Write the equation, substitute with units, rearrange, then answer with units and sensible significant figures.

cards.title: Required practicals in these topics
cards.question: Can you describe the method and sources of error for density and specific heat capacity?
points: Density: ruler or displacement for volume, balance for mass, ρ = m ÷ V.
Specific heat capacity: heater, joulemeter, thermometer, insulated block; c = ΔE ÷ (m Δθ).
Name the independent, dependent and control variables.
Repeat and calculate a mean; identify anomalies.
cards.watch_out: Energy lost to the surroundings makes measured c higher than the true value.
cards.grade9: Suggest one improvement for each source of error.

cards.title: Units and prefixes
cards.question: Can you convert between prefixes and units quickly?
points: kilo (k) = × 10³; mega (M) = × 10⁶; milli (m) = × 10⁻³; micro (µ) = × 10⁻⁶; nano (n) = × 10⁻⁹
Speed: km/h ÷ 3.6 = m/s
cards.watch_out: Area and volume conversions are squared and cubed. 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
cards.grade9: Check units before every calculation; a wrong prefix loses the final mark.

cards.title: Kinetic and gravitational potential energy (booklet gap)
cards.question: How do you calculate kinetic energy and gravitational potential energy, and convert between them?
points: Kinetic energy: Ek = ½ m v². Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times bigger.
Gravitational potential energy: Ep = m g h.
When an object falls, Ep is transferred to Ek (ignoring air resistance), so m g h = ½ m v².
Convert to kJ by dividing by 1000 at the end, not part way through.

example.heading: Booklet question: rocket, 5000 kg at 600 m/s

cards.watch_out: Square the speed only, not the mass: ½ × m × v², so 600² = 360 000 before multiplying.
cards.hook: Half m v squared: only v gets the square.
cards.grade9: In speed kills questions, explain that Ek depends on v², so a small rise in speed gives a big rise in energy transferred in a crash.

cards.title: Efficiency and wasted energy (booklet gap)
cards.question: How do you calculate efficiency, and where does wasted energy go?
points: Efficiency = useful output energy ÷ total input energy (or useful power out ÷ total power in).
Multiply by 100 for a percentage. Efficiency can never be more than 1 (or 100%).
Wasted energy is usually dissipated as thermal energy to the surroundings, for example by friction in a motor.
Reduce waste by lubrication, thermal insulation and using more efficient devices such as LED bulbs.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: A motor uses 500 J and lifts a load gaining 150 J of Ep

cards.watch_out: Put the useful energy on top. An answer over 100% means the fraction is upside down.
cards.grade9: Explain why energy is not lost but dissipated: it spreads into the surroundings and becomes less useful.

cards.title: Conduction, convection and radiation (booklet gap)
cards.question: How does thermal energy transfer, and how do insulation designs reduce it?
points: Conduction: vibrating particles pass energy to neighbours. Fastest in solids, especially metals.
Convection: in liquids and gases, warm fluid expands, becomes less dense and rises; cooler fluid sinks to replace it.
Radiation: infrared waves; needs no particles, so it can cross a vacuum (energy from the Sun to a pool).
A vacuum layer stops conduction and convection. Shiny surfaces reduce radiation. Trapped air is a poor conductor.
cards.watch_out: Immersion heaters sit at the bottom of a tank because hot water rises by convection. Hot water is taken from the top.
cards.hook: Conduction: contact. Convection: currents. Radiation: rays.
cards.grade9: For a vacuum flask or kettle, name each transfer and the feature that reduces it, one by one.

cards.title: Specific heat capacity: multi step questions (booklet gap)
cards.question: How do you answer two and three step heating questions?
points: Rearrange ΔE = m c Δθ for the unknown, then use the answer in the next step.
To find a final temperature, work out Δθ, then subtract it (cooling) or add it (heating).
Link to power: P = E ÷ t, so t = E ÷ P. Convert hours to seconds and kJ to J first.
Give the unit, for example J/kg °C for specific heat capacity.
cards.watch_out: Δθ is the change. The final step (100 − 22) is often missed, losing the last mark.
cards.grade9: Write each step on a new line with the equation first; method marks are awarded even if a later step is wrong.

cards.title: Evaporation and cooling (booklet gap)
cards.question: Why does evaporation cause cooling, for example sweating?
points: Particles in a liquid have a range of energies.
The fastest (most energetic) particles escape from the surface.
The average kinetic energy of the particles left behind falls, so the temperature falls.
Evaporation is faster with a higher temperature, larger surface area, and air movement (wind).
cards.watch_out: Sweat cools you because energy is transferred from the skin to the sweat to evaporate it, not because sweat is cold.
cards.grade9: Use average kinetic energy and temperature in the same sentence to get full marks.

cards.title: The electromagnetic spectrum and wave measurements (booklet gap)
cards.question: What is the order of the EM spectrum, and how do you measure waves in a ripple tank?
points: Order (increasing frequency, decreasing wavelength): radio, microwaves, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X rays, gamma.
All EM waves are transverse and travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
Microwaves heat food because water molecules in the food absorb them. Radio waves have the lowest frequency.
Ripple tank: measure across several waves and divide to find one wavelength; v = f λ.
Echoes: distance = speed × time ÷ 2, because the sound travels there and back (bats, sonar).
cards.watch_out: In echo questions, halve the time or the distance. The sound makes a return trip.
cards.hook: Raging Martians Invaded Venus Using X ray Guns.
cards.grade9: Measuring across 10 waves and dividing reduces the uncertainty compared with measuring one wave.

written.q: Describe how to measure the density of an irregularly shaped stone.
model: Measure the mass on a balance (1)
Fill a eureka can with water up to the spout (1)
Place a measuring cylinder under the spout (1)
Lower the stone in gently and collect the displaced water (1)
Read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus, at eye level (1)
Calculate density = mass ÷ volume; repeat and take a mean (1)

written.q: Explain, using the particle model, why the pressure in a car tyre increases on a hot day.
model: Temperature increases, so particles gain kinetic energy (1)
Particles move faster (1)
They collide with the tyre walls more often (1)
And with more force, so pressure increases (1)

written.q: A diver is 20 m below the surface of sea water (density 1030 kg/m³, g = 9.8 N/kg). Calculate the pressure due to the water.
model: p = h ρ g (1)

written.q: Explain why a ship made of steel floats even though steel is denser than water.
model: Pressure is greater on the bottom of the hull than the top (1)
This gives an upward force, upthrust (1)
The hull shape displaces a large volume of water (1)
Upthrust equals the weight of the ship, so it floats (1)

written.q: Explain why the National Grid uses step-up and step-down transformers.
model: Step-up transformers increase pd for transmission (1)
This reduces the current in the cables (1)
Lower current means less energy lost as heat, so it is more efficient (1)
Step-down transformers reduce pd to 230 V so it is safe for homes (1)

written.q: Describe how to determine the specific heat capacity of an aluminium block.
model: Measure the mass of the block (1)
Insert a heater and thermometer and wrap the block in insulation (1)
Record the starting temperature (1)
Switch on and record energy from a joulemeter (or P × t) after a set time (1)
Record the final temperature and find the change (1)
Calculate c = ΔE ÷ (m × Δθ) (1)

written.q: A car accelerates from 12 m/s to 30 m/s in 6 s. Calculate its acceleration.
model: a = Δv ÷ t (1)

written.q: A skydiver falls at a steady speed. Use Newton's laws to explain why, and describe a Newton's third law pair acting on the skydiver.
model: Air resistance equals weight, so resultant force is zero (1)
By Newton's first law the velocity stays constant (1)
Third law pair: Earth pulls skydiver down, skydiver pulls Earth up (1)
Equal size, opposite direction, same type (gravitational), on different objects (1)

written.q: Booklet style: 46 200 J is transferred from 0.50 kg of water in a kettle in 2 hours. The water starts at 100 °C and c = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the final temperature and the average power output.
model: Final temperature = 78 °C (1)

written.q: Booklet style: a rocket has a mass of 5000 kg and travels at 600 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy in kilojoules.

exam_tips.timing: Section A is 45 questions across all three sciences, so under a minute each. Leave time for Section B.
section_a: Write the equation first, then substitute, then rearrange.
Check prefixes, kPa, cm³ and minutes are the commonest traps.
Cover the options, answer first, then find your answer.
section_b: Particle model answers need a chain, energy, speed, collisions, pressure.
Method questions need equipment, measurements, calculation and how to improve accuracy.
Describe graphs using values from the axes.
grade9: Convert, substitute, calculate, then give the unit. Put 0.35 A into the equation, not 350 mA.
After a calculation, say what it means physically. Zero resultant force means stationary or moving at a constant velocity.
For pressure, check which area the force acts on before using p = F/A.
Ask what the gradient and the area of a graph mean before calculating. The area under a velocity time graph is the distance travelled.
Give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures to match the data.
Practise unfamiliar contexts, such as submarines or weather balloons, and apply the same rules.
week: Most days, 10 to 15 minutes: press Start today (due cards, the new batch, then a short quiz).
Once a week, 15 minutes: one calculation (convert, equation, substitute, answer with unit) and one explain question from Written practice, then mark both.
Once a week: a quiz on the Quiz tab that mixes older units with this week's, so earlier topics stay in.
Fix one mistake: rewrite one wrong answer or one watch out from memory, then check it against the card.

mcq.e: Same mass spread over a bigger volume.

mcq.e: The water displaced equals its volume.

mcq.q: What is 1 g/cm³ in kg/m³?
